title: How Venus Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the planet Venus: its ancient names and observation history, its slow retrograde spin and long day, lack of a magnetic field and moon, the surface's young basalt crust and volcanoes, crushing pressure and extreme heat, the runaway greenhouse effect as a warning for Earth, Soviet and US exploration missions, upcoming Venus missions, and the phosphine biosignature controversy. The episode closes with a listener email about military POG currency.

entities.name: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Venus
segments.summary: Hosts joke about a catchy song, explain why they chose Venus as a topic, and note its paradox as a beautiful-named but hostile planet.

segments.title: Venus names and early observation
segments.summary: Venus is the third brightest object in the sky; Babylonians tracked it as Ishtar; Greeks called it Vesper and Lucifer/Phosphorus until Pythagoras identified one star; Romans named it Venus; features are named after women.

segments.title: Venus orbit, phases and size
segments.summary: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, terrestrial, and orbits inside Earth's orbit so it shows phases; Galileo worked this out in 1610. Venus is similar in size and mass to Earth and is nearly a perfect sphere.

segments.title: Venus spin, magnetic field and missing moon
segments.summary: Venus spins very slowly, about once every 243 Earth days, the slowest in the solar system, so it is nearly spherical. Its core is similar to Earth's but its magnetic field is very weak. Theories suggest Earth's moon once orbited Venus.

segments.title: Retrograde spin theories and day versus year
segments.summary: Venus spins backward relative to Earth. Theories include a slowdown and reversal, or a large impact knocking the planet over, or atmospheric tides. A Venus day of 243 Earth days is longer than its 225-day year; sunrise-to-sunrise is 117 Earth days.

segments.title: Venus surface, crust age and volcanoes
segments.summary: Venus is about 4.8 billion years old, but its crust is only a few hundred million years old, suggesting a global resurfacing. Venus lacks plate tectonics, its crust is mostly basalt, and it has the most volcanoes of any planet, with mountain ranges and highlands. Surface gravity is similar to Earth's.

segments.title: Venus heat and pressure
segments.summary: Surface pressure is about ninety times Earth's, comparable to a kilometer underwater. Surface temperatures are around 800-plus degrees Fahrenheit, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. Kevin McKay's hot plate analogy is cited.

segments.title: Runaway greenhouse effect
segments.summary: Venus is locked in a runaway greenhouse effect: oceans boiled off, water vapor amplified warming, and UV radiation split the vapor so hydrogen escaped, leaving carbon dioxide. The hosts draw a cautionary parallel to Earth's rising CO2 from fossil fuels. Josh mentions his End of the World episode.

segments.title: Sponsor break and self-promotion
segments.summary: Brief promotion for The End of the World with Josh Clark; mid-episode break.

segments.title: Venus atmosphere, clouds and sulfuric acid
segments.summary: The atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen with sulfuric acid clouds and lightning. Upper clouds circulate far faster than surface winds, producing a long-lived polar vortex at the south pole.

segments.title: History of Venus exploration and phosphine controversy
segments.summary: Soviet Venera and Vega missions made early firsts including Venera 4 atmospheric data, Venera 7 soft landing, and Venera 13 audio; US Mariner 2, Pioneer Venus, and Magellan followed. Exploration waned after the Soviet collapse. New NASA missions VERITAS and DaVinci Plus, plus ESA, India, Russia, and Rocket Lab plans are noted. A 2020 phosphine biosignature claim was questioned, possibly confused with sulfur dioxide.

segments.title: Listener mail: POG currency
segments.summary: Listener Jeff recalls Air Force exchange POGs used as change instead of pennies, and a leftover Maggie Simpson POG.
